## 1 Samuel 23 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

### v. 1: *"Now it was reported to David, 'Look, the Philistines are fighting against Keilah and looting the threshing floors.'"*

- **The report came to David, not Saul.** David was already seen by the people as their true protector. Saul was so consumed with hunting David that he had abandoned his royal duty to defend Israel from the Philistines. God was raising up David to act as king before he wore the crown. (Enduring Word) https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-23/
- **Keilah** was a fortified town in the lowlands of Judah, near the Philistine border, south of Adullam. The threshing floors were typically located outside the city gates for wind; the Philistines were seizing the harvested grain. (Gill) https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_samuel/23.htm ; (Ellicott) https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-samuel-23.html
- **The timing:** Harvest was over, and threshing was underway (cf. 2 Samuel 23:13). This made the raid economically devastating. (Gill)

### v. 2: *"So David inquired of the LORD, 'Should I go and attack these Philistines?' And the LORD said to David, 'Go and attack the Philistines and save Keilah.'"*

- **David "inquired of the LORD"** — this is the first of four prayers in the chapter. Matthew Henry notes that David showed his wisdom: some would have dismissed Keilah's need as "not my responsibility" (Saul's job), while others would have rushed in impulsively. David did neither; he sought God. (Enduring Word)
- **How did David inquire?** Ellicott argues it was through the prophet Gad (1 Samuel 22:5), not the Urim and Thummim, since Abiathar only arrived with the ephod later (at Keilah, v. 6). The same formula ("inquired of the LORD") is used of Jehoshaphat inquiring through the prophet Micaiah (1 Kings 22:5–8). (Ellicott) https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-samuel-23.html
- **Gill** notes a different view: some Jewish interpreters (Kimchi, Abarbinel) think Abiathar arrived near Keilah before David entered the city, so the inquiry could have been by Urim and Thummim. The text at v. 6 may be placed to explain the method. (Gill)
- **Matthew Henry** sees David as the protector of the land despite being an outlaw: "Thus did the Saviour Jesus, and left us an example. Those are unlike David, who sullenly decline to do good, if they are not rewarded for services." (Matthew Henry) https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/1_samuel/23.htm

### v. 3: *"But David's men said to him, 'Look, we are afraid here in Judah; how much more if we go to Keilah against the armies of the Philistines?'"*

- **The men's fear was rational.** They were already hunted by Saul in the heart of Judah, where they had friends. Going to Keilah — on the Philistine border — would expose them to a two-front danger: Philistines ahead, Saul behind. (Gill; Enduring Word)
- David was wise to listen to his men's counsel seriously, but he was not ruled by their fear. Guzik notes: "It was good that David became captain over them (1 Samuel 22:2) and that this wasn't a democracy." (Enduring Word)
- **Matthew Henry:** "No sooner did he begin to have soldiers of his own than he found it hard enough to manage them." (Matthew Henry)

### v. 4: *"Once again, David inquired of the LORD, and the LORD answered him: 'Go at once to Keilah, for I will deliver the Philistines into your hand.'"*

- **The second inquiry** was not for David's doubt but for his men's sake — to remove their fears. God confirmed His command and added a specific promise of victory not given the first time. (Gill; Enduring Word)
- **"God likes to confirm His word, especially when He directs us to do something hard or unusual."** (Enduring Word)
- Ellicott again notes this inquiry was also likely through Gad, since Abiathar had not yet arrived. (Ellicott)

### v. 5: *"Then David and his men went to Keilah, fought against the Philistines, and carried off their livestock, striking them with a mighty blow. So David saved the people of Keilah."*

- **Obedience brought victory.** God kept His promise exactly. David's band (now about 600 — v. 13) routed the Philistines, took their livestock, and saved the city. (Enduring Word; Gill)
- The mention of "carried off their livestock" suggests David pursued the Philistines into their own territory — a decisive counter-raid, not merely a defensive action. (Matthew Henry)
- **Precept Austin** notes that David does not act until he knows the Lord's will and that his desire was to "help his fellow countrymen." (Precept Austin, from search excerpt) https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-samuel-23-commentary

### v. 6: *"(Now Abiathar son of Ahimelech had brought the ephod with him when he fled to David at Keilah.)"*

- This parenthetical note is significant for the narrative that follows. Abiathar arrived at Keilah with the high priest's ephod (containing the Urim and Thummim), meaning David now had access to the priestly oracle. (Gill; Matthew Henry)
- **Ellicott** argues the LXX (Septuagint) altered the Hebrew here to say Abiathar "came down *with David* to Keilah," trying to "solve" the difficulty of how David inquired in vv. 2 and 4. But the Hebrew is clear: Abiathar joined David *at* Keilah; the earlier inquiries were through Gad the prophet. (Ellicott)
- **Matthew Henry:** "It was a great comfort to David, in his banishment, that when he could not go to the house of God he had some of the choicest treasures of that house brought to him, the high priest and his breast-plate of judgment." (Matthew Henry)
- **Gill** notes the Hebrew literally reads "the ephod came down in his hand," as though it happened providentially — some Jewish interpreters suggest Abiathar grabbed it in his haste without fully realizing what he carried. (Gill)

### v. 7: *"When Saul was told that David had gone to Keilah, he said, 'God has delivered him into my hand, for he has trapped himself by entering a town with gates and bars.'"*

- **Saul's self-deception.** Saul assumed favorable circumstances meant divine favor. He used pious language ("God has delivered him") to justify murderous intent. He confused military advantage with God's blessing. (Enduring Word)
- **Ellicott** notes the Hebrew word is striking — "God has *repudiated/rejected* him" — and the LXX renders it "sold him" into my hands. Saul deluded himself that his cause was God's cause. (Ellicott)
- **The irony:** Saul would not go to Keilah to fight Philistines (his duty), but he would go to capture David (his obsession). (Enduring Word)

### v. 8: *"Then Saul summoned all his troops to go to war at Keilah and besiege David and his men."*

- Saul's pretext was probably a national war against the Philistines, but his real aim was to trap David. The summons of "all the people" was the royal prerogative; Saul used it for personal vendetta. (Gill; Ellicott)
- **Bridgeway Bible Commentary** notes that David still recognized Saul as legal king and "did not want to fight against him. Nor did he encourage the Israelite people to fight against their king." (Bridgeway) https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bbc/1-samuel-23.html

### v. 9: *"When David learned that Saul was plotting evil against him, he said to Abiathar the priest, 'Bring the ephod.'"*

- Now that Abiathar had arrived with the ephod, David used the Urim and Thummim. The method of inquiry shifts: here the ephod is specifically brought, unlike vv. 2 and 4. (Ellicott)
- **Matthew Henry:** "No sooner is the ephod brought to him than he makes use of it: *Bring hither the ephod.* We have the Scriptures, those lively oracles, in our hands; let us take advice from them in doubtful cases. 'Bring hither the Bible.'" (Matthew Henry)
- **Guzik:** "David was in a bad place, and he was in a bad place because the Lord led him there. Some people might be angry with the Lord but David did the right thing — he inquired of the Lord again." (Enduring Word)

### v. 10–11: David's inquiry: *"Will the citizens of Keilah surrender me into his hand? Will Saul come down…?"* — The LORD: *"He will."*

- **David's questions are inverted in logical order.** The second question (will Saul come down?) should have been first, since the men of Keilah could only surrender David if Saul actually came. This inversion may reflect David's emotional state — his greater concern was the treachery of the city he had just saved. (Ellicott; Gill)
- **The Talmud** (Yoma 73) comments that when two questions are asked together, the Urim and Thummim answers the one that should have been asked first, in proper order. Thus the answer "He will come down" was to the second question David uttered but the first in logical sequence. David then had to repeat the first question in v. 12. (Ellicott)
- **David's concern for the city:** He asks whether Saul will "destroy the city on my account," showing he is more concerned for innocent lives than his own safety. (Matthew Henry)

### v. 12: *"So David asked, 'Will the citizens of Keilah surrender me and my men into the hand of Saul?' 'They will,' said the LORD."*

- **The ingratitude of Keilah.** David had just risked his life to save them from the Philistines, yet they would betray him to Saul. The **Church Pulpit Commentary** calls this "base ingratitude … like that of Judas." (Church Pulpit Commentary, from search excerpt) https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cpc/1-samuel-23.html
- **God's foreknowledge:** Matthew Henry notes, "God knows all men better than they know themselves … He knows not only what will be, but what would be if it were not prevented." (Matthew Henry)
- This was a true conditional prophecy: if David stayed, they would surrender him. God's foreknowledge allowed David to escape. (Enduring Word)

### v. 13: *"Then David and his men, about six hundred strong, set out and departed from Keilah, moving from place to place. When Saul was told that David had escaped from Keilah, he declined to go forth."*

- **David had grown from 400 to 600 men.** No loss from the Philistine battle; in fact, an increase. (Gill)
- **David's humility:** "David could have stood and fought … but David knew that it was not of the Lord and that a lot of innocent people would get hurt in the battle. So David, who was a great warrior, humbled himself and escaped." Guzik compares this to Christ's humble sacrifice. (Enduring Word)
- **"Moving from place to place"** — literally, "went whithersoever they could go." The armed band moved without fixed destination, conducting a kind of border patrol against Philistine raids. (Ellicott; Gill)

### v. 14: *"And David stayed in the wilderness strongholds and in the hill country of the Wilderness of Ziph. Day after day Saul searched for him, but God would not deliver David into his hand."*

- **The Wilderness of Ziph** lies between Hebron and En-gedi — a barren, chalky plateau with deep cliffs. David lived among the strongholds (natural rock fortresses). (Ellicott)
- **"Day after day Saul searched"** — Saul was relentless, obsessed, and derelict in his kingly duties. Yet "God did not deliver him into his hand" — the sovereign hand of God, not David's craftiness, protected him. (Enduring Word; Gill)
- **Ellicott** notes this is a summary statement covering a long period of Saul's reign during which David was perpetually hunted yet divinely protected. (Ellicott)

### v. 15: *"While David was in Horesh in the Wilderness of Ziph, he saw that Saul had come out to take his life."*

- **Horesh** means "wood" or "thicket." Some take it as a proper name for a location; others as simply "in a wood." This provided cover for David and his men. (Ellicott; Gill)
- **Alan Redpath** (quoted in Precept Austin) notes David wrote at least Psalms 27, 31, and 54 during this period — psalms that reveal the spiritual conflict in his heart. (Precept Austin, from search excerpt)

### v. 16: *"And Saul's son Jonathan came to David in Horesh and strengthened his hand in God."*

- **The last meeting of David and Jonathan.** This is their final recorded encounter on earth. Jonathan traveled about 22 miles from Gibeah to find David. (Gill)
- **"Strengthened his hand in God"** — Jonathan could not rescue David practically, but he gave him something more precious: encouragement rooted in faith. The Targum renders it "he strengthened him in the Word of the Lord." (Gill; Enduring Word)
- **Matthew Henry:** "As a pious friend, he directed him to God, the Foundation of his comfort. As a self-denying friend, he takes pleasure in the prospect of David's advancement to the throne." (Matthew Henry)

### v. 17: *"…saying, 'Do not be afraid, for my father Saul will never lay a hand on you. And you will be king over Israel, and I will be your second-in-command. Even my father Saul knows this is true.'"*

- **Three reasons not to fear:** (1) God's protection — Saul would not find him; (2) God's promise — David would be king; (3) loyal friendship — Jonathan would be beside him. (Enduring Word)
- **Jonathan's self-denial:** As crown prince, Jonathan willingly surrendered any claim to the throne. Ellicott notes the pathos — Jonathan would die on Mount Gilboa before David became king, and his dream of being "second-in-command" would never be realized. (Ellicott)
- **"Even my father Saul knows this"** — Saul knew David was the rightful successor (cf. 1 Samuel 15:28; 24:20), yet fought against God's will with everything he had. (Gill; Enduring Word)

### v. 18: *"So the two of them made a covenant before the LORD. And David remained in Horesh, while Jonathan went home."*

- **Covenant renewal** — they had already made a covenant (1 Samuel 18:3; 20:16), but reconfirming it made it "more precious and valid." (Enduring Word)
- Some Jewish interpreters (Kimchi, Abarbinel) suggest "before the LORD" means before Abiathar with the Urim and Thummim. (Gill)
- **This was their last meeting.** "These two dear and cordial friends never saw one another more." (Gill)
- **Matthew Henry:** "Our covenant with God should be often renewed, and therein our communion with him kept up." (Matthew Henry)

### v. 19–20: The Ziphites betray David to Saul: *"Is not David hiding among us … we will be responsible for delivering him into your hand."*

- **Ziph** was in the tribe of Judah — David's own tribe. The Ziphites, terrified by what Saul had done to Nob, chose self-preservation over loyalty to David. (Gill)
- **The contrast:** For every faithful Jonathan, there are Ziphites willing to betray. "Many a godly man or woman has known both friends and betrayers, just as Jesus did." (Enduring Word)
- **The Church Pulpit Commentary** notes the contrast between David's constant reliance on God's guidance and Saul's empty religious language (v. 21). (Church Pulpit Commentary, from search excerpt)

### v. 21: *"'May you be blessed by the LORD,' replied Saul, 'for you have had compassion on me.'"*

- **Saul's spiritual blindness.** He pronounced God's blessing on men who were betraying an innocent man. He was "so spiritually warped" that he saw treason as compassion. (Enduring Word)
- **Matthew Henry:** "In the midst of his wickedness, Saul affected to speak the language of piety. Such expressions, without suitable effects, can only amuse or deceive those who hear, and those who use them." (Matthew Henry)
- Saul complained earlier (1 Samuel 22:8) that no one pitied him. Now he rejoices that the Ziphites do. (Gill)

### v. 22–23: Saul: *"…for I am told that he is extremely cunning. Observe and find out all the places where he hides…"*

- **Saul attributed David's survival to cunning, not to God's protection.** He could not accept that God was guarding David, so he convinced himself David was just "very crafty." (Enduring Word)
- Saul directed the Ziphites to do thorough reconnaissance — find every hiding place, confirm sightings, then return with certainty. He promised to search "all the clans of Judah" (literally "thousands of Judah," the major tribal divisions). (Ellicott; Gill)

### v. 24–25: David moves to the Wilderness of Maon; Saul pursues.

- **Wilderness of Maon** was further south, near the village of Main (modern name), on a conical hill. The "Arabah" is the desolate valley running south from the Dead Sea. (Ellicott)
- David moved to "the rock" — a defensible rocky stronghold. Saul, hearing of it, pursued him there. The cat-and-mouse chase intensified. (Gill)

### v. 26: *"Saul was proceeding along one side of the mountain, and David and his men along the other side. Even though David was hurrying to get away, Saul and his men were closing in on David and his men to capture them."*

- **The closest call.** Saul and David were on opposite sides of the same mountain ridge — perhaps only yards apart — with Saul's forces beginning to encircle David. David was "hurrying" (literally making haste), but the trap was tightening. (Enduring Word; Ellicott)
- This mountain became the emblem of divine intervention — a physical barrier that was about to be overcome when God acted. (Matthew Henry)

### v. 27–28: *"Then a messenger came to Saul, saying, 'Come quickly, for the Philistines have raided the land!' So Saul broke off his pursuit of David and went to meet the Philistines. That is why that place is called Sela-hammahlekoth."*

- **Divine providence at the last moment.** Guzik: "Out of the blue — actually, out of heaven — a messenger came to Saul." The Philistines had likely taken advantage of Saul's southern campaign to invade the north. (Enduring Word; Ellicott)
- **Sela-hammahlekoth** — literally "the rock/cliff of divisions" or "the rock of smoothness/escape." The place was named to commemorate God's deliverance. Ellicott notes alternative interpretations: "Cliff of Destiny/Fate" (Ewald) or "Cliff of Slipping Away." (Ellicott)
- **Matthew Henry:** "Sooner than his promise shall fail, he will commission Philistines to effect our escape, at the very moment when our case appears most desperate." (Matthew Henry)

### v. 29: *"And David went up from there and lived in the strongholds of En-gedi."*

- **En-gedi** — a lush oasis on the western shore of the Dead Sea, with freshwater springs, caves, and steep cliffs. It became David's next refuge and the setting for chapter 24 (where David spares Saul in a cave). (Ellicott; Enduring Word)
- This verse forms a transition: David moved from Maon to the strongholds of En-gedi, where the next dramatic encounter with Saul would occur.

## Distinctive Protestant Traditions

**None of the searches returned explicitly denomination-specific resources with strongly differing interpretations on this chapter** (search limits prevented accessing sites like ligonier.org, desiringgod.org, gty.org, lcms.org, etc.). However, several distinct emphases can be identified across the traditions represented in the sources obtained:

- **Pentecostal/Charismatic (Enduring Word/David Guzik):** Emphasizes David's repeated "inquiring of the Lord" as a model for Spirit-led decision-making; highlights the "providential" nature of the Philistine messenger as a direct divine intervention; strong typological link between David's humble escape and Christ's sacrifice. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-samuel-23/

- **Reformed/Puritan (Matthew Henry):** Emphasizes God's sovereignty in v. 14 ("God delivered him not into his hand") and v. 27 (God "commissioning" the Philistines). Sees David as a type of Christ, the protector of His people. Stresses practical piety: "Bring hither the Bible" as the parallel to "Bring hither the ephod." Views the chapter as illustrating that "the way for any country to be quiet, is to let God's church be quiet in it." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/1_samuel/23.htm

- **Anglican (Ellicott):** Strong on historical-critical detail — the distinction between prophetic inquiry (Gad) and priestly inquiry (Urim and Thummim), discussion of LXX textual variants, geographical identifications, Talmudic commentary. More academic in tone but theologically conservative. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-samuel-23.html

- **Particular Baptist (Gill):** Detailed interaction with rabbinic sources (Kimchi, Abarbinel, the Talmud). Notes that David's deliverance came "just at the nick of time." The Targum's Christological reading of v. 16 ("strengthened him in the Word of the Lord") as referring to "Christ the essential Word of God." https://www.biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_samuel/23.htm

## Summary of Key Themes Across All Sources

1. **David's pattern of inquiry** (vv. 2, 4, 9–12) — four prayers, never acting without knowing God's will. This is the chapter's dominant application point across all traditions.

2. **God's sovereignty over circumstances** — Saul's obsession, Keilah's ingratitude, the Ziphites' betrayal, and the Philistine messenger are all under divine control. "God did not deliver him into his hand" (v. 14) is the theological anchor.

3. **The contrast between Saul and David** — Saul uses religious language without seeking God; David seeks God at every turn. Saul sees Providence as serving his vendetta; David submits to Providence even when it means humbling himself.

4. **Jonathan's friendship** (vv. 16–18) — a model of self-denying, faith-strengthening friendship celebrated across all traditions.

5. **The treachery of Keilah and Ziph** — a sobering note that those you help may betray you, yet God's protection holds.
